```{r setup}
library(variancedonuts)
```

## The idea

When finding the variance, there is a key identity involved which is:

    sum(x^2) = n * mean^2 + sum((x - mean)^2)

The last term is used in most variance formulas. This package draws all three
terms as a square donut. The **whole donut** has area
`sum(x^2)`. The **hole** has area `n * mean^2`. What is left, the **dough**, has
area `sum((x - mean)^2)`, the sum of squared deviations. The variance is the
dough, divided up.

## The Example

The Example data are five numbers.

```{r}
x <- donut_examples$example
x
donut_stats(x)
```

The whole donut is 120, the hole is 80, and the dough is 40.

```{r}
donut_frame(x)
```

The labels give the area and side length of the whole donut and of the hole.
The solid square on the right is a **Berliner**, an all-dough pastry similar
to a donut. It holds exactly the same 40 units of dough, with no hole.

## Dividing the dough

The last line of the picture divides the dough. Divide by `n` for the
population variance and by `n - 1` for the sample variance:

```{r}
st <- donut_stats(x)
st$ss_dev / st$n          # population variance
st$ss_dev / (st$n - 1)    # sample variance
var(x)                    # R's var() divides by n - 1
```

The two variances use the same dough. They differ only in what it is divided
by. The paper calls this choice the baking time.

## Same dough, different donuts

Subtracting 2 from every value moves the mean, so the hole shrinks. The dough
stays the same, so the variance does too.

```{r}
donut_compare(x, donut_examples$example_minus_2, labels = c("x", "x - 2"))
```

`donut_compare()` draws both donuts on one scale, so their areas can be
compared honestly. The verdict below the picture is also kept as an attribute:

```{r}
p <- donut_compare(x, donut_examples$example_minus_2)
attr(p, "verdict")
```

## A donut with no hole

Subtracting 4, the mean, leaves data with mean zero. The hole disappears and
the whole donut is dough: a Berliner, identical to the one drawn beside the
Example donut.

```{r}
donut_frame(donut_examples$berliner, show_sigma = FALSE)
```

## One donut per observation

With `scale = "mean"`, every area is divided by `n`. The whole is the mean of
`x^2`, the hole is the squared mean, and the dough is the population variance
itself. The Berliner's side is then the standard deviation.

```{r}
donut_frame(x, scale = "mean")
donut_stats(x, scale = "mean")
```

## More dough, more variance

Data sets of the same size can be compared by their dough alone.

```{r}
donut_compare(donut_examples$small_mean, x, labels = c("Small mean", "Example"))
```

If the two data sets have different sizes, the donuts on the sum scale also
grow with `n`. `donut_compare()` then gives a warning and compares the
variances instead. Use `scale = "mean"` to compare such data sets fairly.

## The coefficient of variation

The ratio of the dough to the empty center is the squared coefficient of
variation, with the
standard deviation computed using divisor `n`:

```{r}
st <- donut_stats(x)
st$ss_dev / (st$n * st$mean^2)   # dough / hole
(sqrt(st$variance) / st$mean)^2  # CV squared
```

A large empty center with little dough around it means a small coefficient of
variation.

## Glaze-thin donuts

When the mean is large compared with the spread, the hole fills almost the
whole donut, and the dough is a thin glaze.

```{r}
g <- donut_examples$glaze_thin
donut_stats(g)
donut_frame(g, show_sigma = FALSE)
```

This is where the shortcut formula `sum(x^2) - n * mean^2` gets into trouble.
It subtracts two huge, nearly equal areas, and the computer's rounding errors
can swamp the thin dough. Shift the glaze-thin data far enough and the
shortcut fails:

```{r}
far <- g + 1e8
mean(far^2) - mean(far)^2       # the shortcut: wrong
donut_stats(far)$variance       # the careful way: 0.02
```

`donut_stats()` always computes the dough from squared deviations, so its
answer stays right. It also flags data that are close to this boundary, as the
printout shows:

```{r}
donut_stats(g + 1e6)
```

The whole and the hole print as the same 13-digit number. They really are
equal to that many digits, and the dough of 0.1 is the tiny difference between
them. That is the shortcut formula's problem in one line.

## Colors

So far every donut has been plain golden, the default. Ten color schemes are
available, by number or name:

```{r}
donut_schemes()[, c("id", "name")]
```

Schemes 3 to 6 add a stripe of pink or white glaze. It is decoration only and
changes no area.

```{r}
donut_frame(x, color = "golden_pinkglaze")
```

Scheme 7 adds sprinkles:

```{r}
donut_frame(x, color = 7)
```

Schemes 8 to 10 are flavors, with the dough one color all over: strawberry,
chocolate and vanilla.

```{r}
donut_frame(x, color = "chocolate")
```

Two data sets can be drawn in different colors. Use this only for genuinely
different groups, because different colors can suggest a difference that is
not there.

```{r}
donut_compare(x, donut_examples$example_minus_2, color = c(3, 7),
              labels = c("Group A", "Group B"))
```

## Saving pictures

The functions return ggplot objects, so `ggplot2::ggsave()` saves them. The
labels use Greek letters, which R's basic `pdf()` device cannot draw. Save as
PNG, or as PDF with `device = cairo_pdf`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
p <- donut_frame(x)
ggplot2::ggsave("donut.png", p, width = 6.5, height = 4)
ggplot2::ggsave("donut.pdf", p, width = 6.5, height = 4, device = cairo_pdf)
```
